messages.subject: Can Someone Run a Quick Test For Me?
parts:
Using any Stan model can you hack any method to print out the results of lp in each of these calls?

stan::model::gradient(model_, cont_params_, lp, init_grad, &std::cout);
lp = model_.template log_prob<true, true>(cont_params_, &std::cout);

lp = model_.template log_prob<false, true>(cont_params_, &std::cout);
lp = model_.template log_prob<false, false>(cont_params_, &std::cout);

The absolute values don’t matter — I’m just looking for the comparison.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Can Someone Run a Quick Test For Me?
parts:
I used a model with a constraint so there was a non-empty
Jacobian and ran with both double and var inputs where
appropriate. I attached the model and C++ with added main()
to run it.

Recall that the template params are

<propto,apply_jacobian>


~/temp2$ ./formichael

DOUBLE
stan::model::gradient, lp = -4.46842
<true,true> lp = 1
<true,false> lp = 0
<false,true> lp = -8.14418
<false,false> lp = -9.14418

VAR
<true,true> lp = -4.46842:0
<true,false> lp = -5.46842:0
<false,true> lp = -8.14418:0
<false,false> lp = -4.46842:0


It looks like gradient and the var-based <true,true> match,
as expected.

Propto with all doubles causes everything to drop out other
than the Jacobian (when activated).

I'm worried about the mismatch in <false,false> (which should
not drop constants and should not include the jacobian, but it
turns out to be equivalent to the <true,true> case.

This is why I was thinking it'd make sense to include as a unit
test the cases that are expected to be the same.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Can Someone Run a Quick Test For Me?
parts:
The <true,false> case being zero for double makes sense.  Terms in PDFs are dropped when propto=true and the data type that they'd produce is a double.  Calling the double version with propto=true means that *everything* results in a double, so basically it removes the ability of the PDFs to tell what's a constant.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Follow-up on log_prob calculation
parts:
On Jul 27, 2014, at 5:03 PM, Alp Kucukelbir <akucu...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Michael, Bob:

We're not the only ones who understand this bit of the code!
> This was super-helpful. I wasn't even aware of the distinction between the "DOUBLE" and "VAR" cases described above.

If propto=true, Stan drops constants, defined as any term in the log prob
that doesn't involve a var or fvar (fvar is the type for forward-mode
autodiff, which lets us do higher-order derivatives).

> OK so my question to everyone now is this: I want to get the version of log_prob that corresponds to Bob's "VAR<true, true>" case. But I don't want to compute a gradient (at that point in the code).
>
> Can I do this with double (in Eigen Vector/Matrix/whatever) inputs?
No. See the definition of propto above.
> Or do I need to convert my inputs to stan::agrad::var objects? (If the latter, how should I go about doing that efficiently/safely?)

Use the double-based log_prob_propto function in model/util.hpp.

It only does the forward-pass part of reverse-mode. We could probably
rewrite it to just use forward-mode, which should be more efficient.

- Bob

On Jul 27, 2014, at 7:23 PM, Alp Kucukelbir <akucu...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I don't believe I will need the normalization at this point, as I'm computing a lower bound.
>
> I've implemented a "hacky" version in src/stan/vb/bbvb.hpp, function calc_ELBO. (This is on the feature/bbvb branch.)
>
> I will to look into Bob's suggestion of doing this without casting everything to a stan::agrad::var.

It does the promotion to stan::agrad::var behind the scenes. It
just avoids the backward pass that applies the chain rule.

If you can, you want to combine the computation of the log prob
and the gradient.

The only way to get around this performance hit would be to rewrite
all of our probability functions to do templating for dropping terms
in a more refined way than just looking at the types. Not impossible,
but a lot of work.

- Bob
